pair.title: Same observer, same target, one assumption changed
pair.mini: Same eye height, same distance, same target height. Only the shape of the ground changes, and with it the elevation angle α at which the target is seen.
pair.text: One observer, one target, one ground distance, one target height, identical in both panels. Only the shape of the ground differs. On a plane, the target's elevation angle α follows from the heights and the distance alone. On a globe, the target also drops below the observer's horizontal by the curvature, about d²/2R, so the same target is seen at a lower angle, and far enough away, below eye level. The dashed line is eye level, and α is drawn at the same radius in both panels so the two can be compared by eye. Distances are schematic.
pair.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: distant summits measured at the plane's elevation angles rather than the globe's.
land.title: The view from the Sommet de Viériou, from LiDAR
land.mini: The landscape from the Sommet de Viériou (1,395 m), drawn from the IGN's 1 m LiDAR, with a photograph from the summit fading over it. The globe, with and without refraction, and the plane, one above the other.
land.text: The landscape seen from the Sommet de Viériou (1,395 m [2]), in the Alpes-Maritimes, drawn from the IGN's LiDAR HD terrain model [1]. Each band of colour is the highest ridge within one range of distance, from 0.5 to 120 km, pale far off and dark close by. The Castellaras (17.7 km, 1,400 m [3]) and the Cime de Barbin (60 km, 1,561 m) sit at the elevation angles each model gives them, in three views one above the other: the globe with refraction, with straight rays, and the plane. A photograph taken from the summit fades in and out. It was aligned by computation, not by hand: azimuth and scale from a search against the LiDAR skyline, and the camera's unrecorded tilt set for each model at its most favourable value. The landscape is decor; the test is the named summits.
land.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the photographed summits sitting where the plane puts them, the Barbin above the Castellaras.
arg.title: The Argentera behind the Riourun, from a roadside
arg.mini: From a roadside at 105 m, the Argentera (64 km, 3,297 m) appears just beside the Riourun (17 km). The photograph's skyline matches the globe to 0.65′ and the plane to 4.1′.
arg.text: From a roadside at 105 m (43.62258° N, 7.07217° E), a camera aimed at 17.6° shows the Argentera, the highest summit of the Maritime Alps (3,297 m [2]), 64 km away in Italy, just left of the Riourun, 17 km away. The landscape is drawn from the IGN's LiDAR HD [1]. The photograph's scale comes from the camera's focal length, the same for every model; its azimuth is anchored on the Argentera's summit, which every model puts at the same bearing; tilt and height are then fitted for each model, in its favour. Its skyline matches the globe's to 0.65′ and the plane's to 4.1′. The order of the two summits settles it: the Riourun stands 3.2′ above the Argentera once the tilt is removed. The globe predicts +1.3′ to +5.7′; the plane −7.2′ to −9.9′, with the Argentera on top.
arg.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the Argentera photographed above the Riourun, as the plane predicts.
sil.title: One terrain, two models: the Cime de Barbin changes sign
sil.mini: The skyline from the Sommet de Viériou, read off 1 m LiDAR. A plane puts the Cime de Barbin, 60 km away, 9.5′ above eye level. A globe puts it 4.6′ below. Fourteen arcminutes and a change of sign.
sil.text: The skyline seen from the Sommet de Viériou (1,395 m [2]), swept off the IGN's LiDAR HD terrain [1], not drawn by hand: one terrain, two models, 6.2° of azimuth centred on the Castellaras [3]. Both axes are at true angular scale, with no exaggeration, so the panorama is a low band, as a photograph shows it. The filled outline is the globe with standard refraction (k = 0.13); the dashed line is the same terrain with the curvature removed. The Cime de Barbin, at 60 km, sits 9.5′ above eye level on a plane and 4.6′ below it on a globe. Its height above the dips beside it (about 16′) is the same in both models: the test is height above the horizontal, not above a neighbour. The terrain model reads the three summits within 1.5 m of their published heights.
sil.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the Cime de Barbin seen above eye level from the Sommet de Viériou.
flatten.title: Flatten the Earth, and two summits swap
flatten.mini: From the Sommet de Viériou, the Cime de Barbin (60 km) sits 2.8′ below the Castellaras (17.7 km) on the globe, and 8.5′ above it on a plane. Flatten the Earth and they swap.
flatten.text: From the Sommet de Viériou (1,395 m [1]), the Castellaras (17.7 km, 1,400 m [2]) and the Cime de Barbin (60.0 km, 1,561 m) stand almost in line. On the globe, the far Barbin sits 2.8′ below the Castellaras with straight rays, 1.4′ with standard refraction (k = 0.13). On a plane it rides 8.5′ above. The animation flattens the Earth step by step: the two tops are level at 75% of the real curvature, a sphere of about 8,500 km radius. The sign flip needs no plane, only an Earth a third larger. The angles in the eye view are true; only the spacing of the peaks is schematic.
flatten.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the Barbin seen above the Castellaras from the Sommet de Viériou.
twoangles.title: A summit's height from two angles
twoangles.mini: Two elevation angles taken a known distance apart give a summit's height without climbing it. On a plane, two textbook formulas must agree. On the real Earth they do not.
twoangles.text: The surveyor's "inaccessible height": measure a summit's elevation angle from two stations a known distance apart, and its height follows without reaching it. There are two textbook ways to compute it, the tangent method and the law of sines. On a genuine plane they are algebraically the same, so they must return the same height. Fed the angles a distant summit really produces, they disagree. That disagreement is only possible if the two stations' level references are not parallel, which is curvature, measured. The drawing is schematic.
twoangles.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the tangent and law-of-sines heights agreeing for distant summits, as they must on a plane.
frames.title: Same triangle, two reference frames
frames.mini: The law of sines holds for any triangle, flat ground or not. What the globe changes is where each angle is measured from: the level at one station is tilted from the level at the other.
frames.text: Three points, the observer O, a near station N and a target T, always make a triangle, and the law of sines holds for it whatever the ground does. What curvature changes is the direction each angle is measured from. On a plane, the level at N is parallel to the level at O. On a globe it is rotated by the angle between the two places at the Earth's centre. The tangent method assumes the two levels are parallel; the law of sines only needs the triangle. So on a globe the two methods give different heights, and the size of the difference measures the tilt. The drawing is schematic.
frames.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the level at distant stations measured parallel to the local level.
tangents.title: An angle can be measured on a ball
tangents.mini: Two protractors on one sphere, each with 0° along its own horizontal. Both work normally. What the curvature does is tilt the two 0° lines apart, by the angle between the two places.
tangents.text: A common objection holds that angles only mean something on a flat plane. But an angle is measured from a reference direction, and every point on a sphere has one: the horizontal a bubble level settles into, the tangent at your feet. Here one protractor stands at the observer and one on a summit, each with 0° along its own tangent. Both read ordinary angles. The curvature tilts the two 0° lines relative to each other, by exactly the angle between the two places at the Earth's centre. The mountain is drawn absurdly large, 30% of the planet's radius, so the angles are legible.
tangents.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the horizontals of two distant places measured parallel.
recip.title: Two zenith angles, no free parameter
recip.mini: Two stations measure the zenith angle to each other at the same moment. On a plane the two always add up to exactly 180°. On a globe they exceed 180° by the angle between the stations.
recip.text: Two stations point at each other and each reads the zenith angle, the angle down from straight up, at the same moment. On a plane every vertical is parallel, so the two readings add up to exactly 180°, at any distance and for any heights: the flat prediction has nothing to adjust. On a globe the two verticals meet at the centre, so the sum exceeds 180° by the angle between the stations, d/R. Refraction reduces the excess to about (d/R)(1 − k), and because simultaneous readings share nearly the same air, this is also how geodesists measure k. No value of k brings the excess back to zero. The drawing is schematic.
recip.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: simultaneous reciprocal zenith angles adding to exactly 180° over long distances.
size.title: The globe moves summits, it does not shrink them
size.mini: Between the two models, a distant peak's apparent size changes by at most 0.011%. Its position against eye level changes by up to 14.1′. The curve moves where things sit, not how big they look.
size.text: If the Earth were curved, would mountains look wrong in photographs? No. The two models disagree about where a peak sits in the view, but almost not at all about how big it looks. For the summits in this example, apparent size differs by at most 0.011% between the models, a fraction of an arcsecond, far below what a lens or an eye resolves. Position against eye level differs by up to 14.1′, hundreds of times more. That is why the test needs a level and a protractor rather than a camera: mountains looking normal says nothing about the shape of the ground. The drawing is schematic.
size.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: distant summits sitting at the heights against eye level that the plane predicts.
schnee.title: The Schneeberg from Vienna, 71 km away
schnee.mini: From Vienna, the Schneeberg (2,076 m) rises 71 km away behind the Anninger's wooded ridge. Fitted to the Austrian LiDAR skyline, deprojected's photograph puts that ridge 1′ to 2.5′ from the globe and 13′ from the plane.
schnee.text: From Vienna at 164 m, deprojected photographed the Schneeberg, the highest summit of Lower Austria (Klosterwappen, 2,076 m [2]), 71 km away, rising behind the wooded ridge of the Anninger (675 m [3]), 26 km away. The landscape is drawn from the Austrian BEV's 1 m laser-scan terrain model [1], three times: the globe with refraction, with straight rays, and the plane. The photograph is anchored on the summit, which every model puts at the same bearing; scale, tilt and height are fitted for each model, in its favour. The dark ridge in front, never used in the fit, then falls 1′ from the globe with straight rays, 2.5′ from the globe with refraction (the terrain model has no trees, and the forest adds up to about 3′) and 13′ from the plane, which would put it below the bottom of the frame. The viewpoint and eye height are as given by deprojected.
schnee.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the dark ridge photographed about 27′ below the Schneeberg's summit, as the plane predicts, rather than 15′ to 16′.
